methodological_rigor.justification: Secondary analysis of Phase 2 trial (n=37 primary, n=118 with pseudo-labeling) examining deep learning segmentation and radiomics. Small sample size (n=37 test cases) with limited external validation. Appropriate statistical methods: paired t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, ICC ≥0.8, Spearman ≤0.95 for feature selection. However, acknowledged limitations: segmentation performed on T2WIs but models trained on sDWIs/ADC maps (spatial mismatch); pseudo-labeled data inherent errors; single-center with no external validation. Post-treatment segmentation performance substantially degraded, though inter-rater agreement similarly declined.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Diagnostic/prognostic study (LoE 4) from Phase 2 trial addressing clinically important question of non-operative management selection for rectal cancer via cCR prediction. Radiomics clustering showed distinction between cCR/non-cCR but validation requires larger studies. Limited clinical translation readiness due to small sample, single-center design, and acknowledged need for multi-institutional validation before implementation.

reporting_quality.justification: Comprehensive methods reporting of MRI protocols, DWI calculations, nnU-Net architecture, image preprocessing (SimpleITK details), and statistical analyses. Transparent acknowledgment of limitations including spatial mismatch, single radiologist training bias, and post-treatment challenges. Code availability statement provided (GitHub repository referenced). Follows modified TRIPOD elements; registration/image alignment limitations explicitly discussed. High transparency regarding modeling assumptions and limitations.

novelty_literature.justification: nnU-Net for rectal tumor segmentation is established methodology applied to new clinical context (post-treatment assessment, non-operative selection). Semi-supervised learning with pseudo-labeled data demonstrates practical approach to limited annotation problem, but conceptually incremental. Radiomic clustering for treatment response prediction in rectal cancer is relatively novel within this specific indication, extending existing radiomics literature to MRI-based assessment.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear motivation, comprehensive methods including preprocessing details, honest results presentation showing both successes (pre-treatment) and challenges (post-treatment), and thoughtful discussion acknowledging limitations. Appropriate use of figures (segmentation examples, clustering heatmap) and tables. Limitations section is extensive and transparent regarding spatial mismatch, small sample size, and generalizability concerns. Publication-ready clarity.

key_strengths: Transparent reporting of both successes (pre-treatment segmentation, Model 2 semi-supervised improvement) and failures (post-treatment degradation equal to human raters), demonstrating methodological honesty
Semi-supervised learning approach with pseudo-labeled data (n=81) addressing practical scarcity of annotated medical imaging data; Model 2 achieved radiologist-level agreement on pre-treatment cases
Comprehensive statistical analysis including paired t-tests, Wilcoxon tests, bootstrapped confidence intervals, and appropriate feature selection (ICC, Spearman filtering)
Code availability and explicit BioRender acknowledgments; good reproducibility documentation including Python versions and SimpleITK specifications
key_concerns: Small sample size (n=37 test cases) from single center; multi-institutional external validation essential before clinical implementation
Acknowledged spatial mismatch: segmentation delineated on T2WIs but models trained on sDWIs/ADC maps; conventional registration insufficient, limiting reliability of integrated pipeline
Post-treatment segmentation performance poor (DSC 0.175-0.362) for both Model 3 and human raters; acknowledged but unresolved; applicability to watch-and-wait surveillance limited

Model 2 trained bias: 97.3% improvement vs radiologist but only 59.5% vs fellow, suggesting model learned radiologist-specific patterns rather than generalizable segmentation; multi-radiologist training would strengthen
chief_reviewer.rationale: Well-executed proof-of-concept study with strong transparency about limitations. Pre-treatment segmentation and radiomics clustering show promise; post-treatment challenges acknowledged honestly. Suitable for Tier 3 with minor revisions addressing spatial mismatch resolution and post-treatment improvements.
